Within 6 months of the termination of the stressor or its consequences

S081.name: Stress_Related_Maladaptive_Response
S081.description: Emotional or behavioral symptoms appearing in response to an identifiable stressor.

subtypes.With Depressed Mood: Symptoms mainly include low mood, tearfulness, or feelings of hopelessness.
subtypes.With Anxiety: Symptoms mainly include nervousness, worry, jitteriness, or separation anxiety.
subtypes.With Mixed Anxiety and Depressed Mood: A combination of depression and anxiety symptoms appears.
subtypes.With Disturbance of Conduct: Symptoms mainly involve violation of rules, truancy, vandalism, reckless driving, or fighting.
subtypes.With Mixed Disturbance of Emotions and C: Both emotional symptoms (depression, anxiety) and behavioral problems appear together.
subtypes.Unspecified: Maladaptive reactions not classified into the above types (e.g., physical complaints, social withdrawal).

symptom.disease_info: Adjustment Disorder is characterized by the development of emotional or behavioral symptoms in response to an identifiable psychosocial stressor, with onset typically within 3 months of the stressor and clinically significant distress or functional impairment out of proportion to what would be expected. It often presents with anxiety, low mood, or mixed disturbance of emotions and conduct, but does not meet full criteria for another mental disorder and does not represent a normal bereavement reaction. The course is usually self-limited, resolving within 6 months after the stressor or its consequences have ended, though it can become chronic if stressors persist. Clinically, it is distinguished from normative stress reactions by its impact on social, occupational, or academic functioning and from major depressive or anxiety disorders by its subthreshold, stressor-linked symptom profile and time course.

patient.stressor: About a month ago, Patricia’s company lost a major contract and abruptly announced a restructuring that moved her from her long-standing fabrication team to a different shift and supervisor, cutting back on the creative custom projects she cherished. The new role emphasized repetitive production work with tighter quotas and less autonomy, and it conflicted with her established routines at home and in her studio, where she usually spent evenings on metal sculptures and weekend gallery visits along the Charleston waterfront. Over the next several weeks, she found herself staying late to meet unfamiliar production targets, cancelling paddle-boarding and pickleball, and letting commissioned art pieces sit half-finished, which strained her relationship with clients and led to pointed feedback from her new boss. When she began contemplating quitting despite needing the income and her spouse noticed how much the job change was disrupting their household and her once-reliable functioning, she agreed to see a mental health provider through the employee assistance program to address how poorly she was adapting to the workplace changes.
patient.chief_complaint: “Ever since they changed my position at the shop, I just can’t seem to adjust, and it’s throwing off my work and my whole routine.”
